26-189 - Resolution to Celebrate and Honor the Transition and Closure of the 
Congregational Church of West Medford, Sanctuary United Church of Christ 
Offered by Isaac Bears, Council President, Matt Leming, City Councilor, Liz Mullane, City 
Councilor 
 
Whereas, the Congregational Church of West Medford, Sanctuary United Church of Christ has 
served as a heart of the Medford faith community for 154 years; and 
 
Whereas, a final act of public ministry and closing worship and celebration was held on October 
17th; and 
 
Whereas, we honor, grieve, celebrate, and reflect on the deeply meaningful role of this faith 
community in our city’s history; now, therefore: 
 
Be it Resolved by the Medford City Council that we celebrate and thank all of the residents who 
have been part of the Congregational Church of West Medford, Sanctuary United Church of 
Christ community. 
 
Be it Further Resolved that we honor the continued leadership of Reverend Wendy Miller 
Olapade as a faith leader in our community and thank her and the members of the Sanctuary 
UCC Legacy Team for their work to celebrate their community during this transition and closure. 
Callahan. Approved on a Voice Vote of Seven in favor, Zero opposed. 
 
President Bears read the following letter from Kim Grubb into the record: 
 
Remarks Regarding the Resolution Recognizing the Closing of the Congregational Church of 
West Medford 
  
I would like to speak regarding the resolution recognizing the closing of the Congregational 
Church of West Medford. I am sure that those who are putting forward this resolution may be 
focusing primarily on the last 13 years of the church’s history. However, I feel it is important to 
recognize and remember all the years that came before, under the leadership of the many 
ministers who helped shape this church and its place in the community.
The Congregational Church of West Medford, or CCWM, has a history spanning more than 150 
years. Its story began with a woman named Rachel Barnes, who started a Sunday school in her 
home so that children in West Medford would not have to walk all the way to Medford Square or 
Arlington to attend Sunday school. That simple act of caring for children was the beginning of 
something that would become an important part of the community for generations. 
 
In June 1872, residents of West Medford founded the Congregational Church of West Medford. 
At the time, there was already a Mystic Congregational Church in Medford Square. A wooden 
church with a steeple was built at Harvard and Bower Streets, on the site where the fire station 
stands today. The church’s bell became the community’s fire alarm, and its clock served as the 
timepiece for West Medford. 
 
From its earliest days, the church was much more than a place of worship. It was an important 
part of everyday life in the community. Between 1889 and 1895, under the leadership of the 
Reverend Herbert Warner Stebbens, the church experienced an extraordinary period of growth. 
Carriages and barges were sent to Hillside to bring people who were lame or convalescing to 
Sunday morning services. The cost was 20 cents per person each way. A committee was 
established to help unemployed people find jobs, and an Athletic Association was formed, which 
was later taken over by the town. Sunday school enrollment reached 381 children, and the 
church had two large choirs. 
 
These accomplishments tell us something important about the church. Its mission extended 
beyond its own congregation. It was a place where people came together to care for one 
another and meet the needs of the wider community. 
  
On March 4, 1903, tragedy struck when the church burned to the ground after its bell sounded 
the first alarm. But the congregation did not give up. The parishioners came together, 
determined to rebuild. Just two years later, they dedicated a new granite church at 400 High 
Street. The city helped pay for a clock in the new steeple, and its clock and chimes continued to 
mark the time for the people of West Medford. 
 
The church prospered after the First World War and again after the Second World War. In 1954, 
the Parish House was added, providing even more space for the congregation and its activities. 
Throughout its history, CCWM continued to find ways to serve its community. In the early 
1970s, an associate minister helped run a weekend drop-in space for teenagers, providing 
young people with a place to gather. The church’s ninth minister, Dr. Gordon Washburn, served 
for more than 35 years. He was also a member of the Medford School Committee in the late 
1960s and early 1970s. He was deeply invested in the community and always willing to help 
wherever he could. 
 
That spirit of service continued through the many programs and organizations that called 
CCWM home. These included Community Family, an adult day care program; Gentle Dragon 
Preschool; Bright Stars Afterschool Program for elementary-age children; Alcoholics 
Anonymous; and Scout troops as well as Campfire Girls and Boys . The church also hosted an 
innovative group called New Beginnings for people who were recently divorced. 
Through English at Large, volunteers helped immigrants learn English and offered other forms 
of support as they adjusted to life in this country. 
  
And, of course, CCWM was known as the "eatingest church in Medford! " We hosted countless 
community gatherings and meals, including lobster luncheons, Finnan Haddie dinners, pancake 
breakfasts, Easter breakfasts, and turkey dinners. One of the biggest events was the annual 
Church Fair, which brought everyone together. Members prepared food, knitted items, and 
contributed all sorts of treasures for the ever-popular White Elephant Room. We held many 
Bible studies to bring us closer to Christ, for all members and most recently before we sold the 
church building the creation of The Lakota Youth Stay Program that is still run by some past 
members of CCWM on their own. 
 
These events were about more than raising money. They brought people together, created 
friendships, and made the church a welcoming place for the community. The music program 
was so beautiful and would just draw people in. 
  
Now, I would like to share why this history means so much to me personally. I was born into this 
church in 1958. As soon as I was old enough, I became involved in volunteering in just about 
every aspect of church life. I taught Sunday school for more than 30 years, sang in the choir, 
and served on numerous committees alongside so many wonderful people. My weeks were 
filled with meetings, teaching Sunday school, and working with youth groups.
I could go on and on about my experiences and memories from over 60 years of being a 
member and attended CCWM, including the years before we sold the building. This church was 
not simply somewhere I went on Sundays. It was a major part of my life, my family, and my 
identity. 
 
One of the things that made CCWM so special was its people. Over the years, people came and 
went, but the friendships and connections remained meaningful. My children grew up knowing 
many of the wonderful people I had grown up with. Even those who were part of the church for 
only a short time became part of that caring community. 
 
It was a place where people cared about their faith, helped their neighbors, supported one 
another, and genuinely wanted to make a difference. And when you give of yourself in that way, 
it often comes back to you in ways you could never have imagined. 
I remember one elderly woman who had been a member of the church years earlier. No one 
asked her about her financial circumstances, but members assumed she was living on a fixed 
income. They quietly brought her food and clothing and made sure she had rides to church. 
They did these things simply because they cared about her. 
When she passed away, the church learned that she had left it more than one million dollars. 
Everyone was shocked. Her generosity helped the church continue on, even as membership 
declined. 
 
I have always thought that this story captures the heart of CCWM. This woman had been 
welcomed and cared for without question or expectation. In return, she chose to leave a 
remarkable gift to the church she loved. 
 
That was the kind of community we had. People looked out for one another, not because they 
expected anything in return, but because that was who they were. 
I am incredibly grateful for the years I spent at CCWM, for the opportunity to serve, for the 
friendships I made, and for the many memories that I will always carry with me. It is 
heartbreaking that the church is now gone, but the impact it had on so many lives cannot be 
erased. 
 
As we recognize the closing of the Congregational Church of West Medford, I hope we will 
remember its entire history—not just its final 13 years. We should remember the people who 
built it, the ministers who led it, the generations who worshipped there, the children who learned 
there, the volunteers who gave their time, and the countless people in the community who 
benefited from its presence. 
CCWM was a place of faith, service, generosity, friendship, and love. It was part of the fabric of 
West Medford for more than 150 years. 
 
CCWM may be gone, but the history, the contributions, and the memories remain. 
This is what the Congregational Church of West Medford was all about, and this is the legacy I 
hope we will recognize and honor. 
Thank you. 
Kim Grubb

Time for Employees of the City of Medford," to the Admin & Finance Committee;

26-190 - Resolution to Support the United Labor of Tufts Resident Assistants in Their 
Negotiations for a Fair Contract 
Offered by Matt Leming, City Councilor, Isaac Bears, Council President 
 
WHEREAS The United Labor of Tufts Resident Assistants previously negotiated a fair contract 
with Tufts University; 
 
WHEREAS The Tufts Resident Assistants are working to renew that contract to account for 
drastically increasing costs of living; 
 
WHEREAS Tufts University, without the input of Resident Assistants, is proposing to decrease 
the hours of RAs, cut into the work they're expected to do, and decrease compensation while 
transferring these responsibilities to non-unionized professional staff; 
 
WHEREAS Resident Assistants provide essential support to students by fostering safe, 
welcoming residential communities and helping students navigate the challenges of college life; 
 
WHEREAS The housing and compensation provided to Resident Assistants help make their 
education more affordable in an area where the cost of living is increasingly prohibitive; 
 
WHEREAS Meaningful collective bargaining requires that Resident Assistants have a genuine 
voice in decisions affecting their working conditions, responsibilities, and compensation; 
 
BE IT RESOLVED that the Medford City Council offer its full and unconditional support of the 
Tufts Resident Assistants in their fight for a fair contract and denounce any further anti-labor 
practices from the University. 
 
Addressing the Council: 
Carly Hope, United Labor of Tufts RA’s

26-187 - Resolution to Develop an Ordinance for the Banning of Black Plastic Takeout 
Containers from Medford Restaurants 
Offered by Matt Leming, City Councilor, Anna Callahan, City Councilor 
 
WHEREAS, a recent study found that black plastic takeout containers contain toxic flame 
retardants that bear high risk of seeping into food; and 
 
WHEREAS, the Medford Board of Health recently sent a letter to restaurants recommending 
that they convert away from black plastic takeout containers in favor of clear plastic; 
 
BE IT RESOLVED that the Medford City Council develop an ordinance formalizing the transition 
away and ban of black plastic takeout containers from our City; 
 
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that this be referred to the Medford Energy and Environment 
Committee for recommendations and drafting of an ordinance.

24-047 - Resolution to Request Linkage Fee Updates in Medford 
Offered by Matt Leming, City Councilor 
 
PART II - REVISED ORDINANCES 
Chapter 94 - ZONING 
SECTION 94-10.0. DEVELOPMENT LINKAGE FEES 
 
 
SECTION 94-10.0. DEVELOPMENT LINKAGE FEES
Sec. 94-10.1. Parks and recreational facilities. 
94-10.1.1 Purpose. The purpose of this section is to promote the public health, safety, 
convenience and welfare; to prevent the deterioration of existing parks and public recreational 
facilities; to establish a balance between real estate development and the open space and 
recreational needs of city residents; and to mitigate the impacts of future development on the 
deterioration of parks and public recreational facilities, by provisions designed to:  
1. Afford review and regulation of real estate development projects which directly or 
indirectly lead to conditions of the use of parks and public recreational facilities that 
contribute to an increase in the costs for the upgrade, repair and maintenance of parks 
and public recreational facilities, and the need for new capital improvements.  
2. Provide a fund for parks and public recreational facility capital improvements through a 
linkage grant to the park and recreational facilities trust, as a condition of the approval of 
any nonresidential development of 10,000 square feet of gross floor area or more; any 
residential development of six units or more; any subdivision of property which creates 
six or more units or buildable lots; or any residential or nonresidential project requiring a 
density bonus, variance, special permit, or zoning map amendment that is requested for 
a project of 5,000 square feet or more except those that are exempt pursuant to section 
94-10.1.4. Requests for such zoning relief may include bonuses in density of use such as 
increases in gross floor area, height or other changes in dimensional requirements.  
3. The imposition of linkage fees is one of the preferred methods of ensuring that 
development bears a proportionate share of the cost of capital facilities necessary to 
accommodate such development. This must be done in order to promote and protect the 
public health, safety and welfare.  
4. The methodology and analysis for the determination of the impact of new development, 
the need for new facilities and their costs, and the establishment and calculation of the 
linkage fees shall be established as a result of an investigation and report with supporting 
documentation, which shall be available for inspection by any feepayer or the public.  
Calculations of linkage fees may be based on the methodology established by previous 
studies that outline methods for an escalating linkage fee formula. 
5. The provisions of this section shall be construed so as to effectively carry out its purpose 
in the interest of the public health, safety and welfare.  
94-10.1.2 Definitions. See section 94-12.0, "Development linkage fees".  
94-10.1.3 Procedures. The  mayor or the office of community developmentcommunity 
development board  shall be empowered to promulgate regulations and establish fees it deems 
necessary to implement this section. For a development impact project, no building permit or 
density bonus, variance, special permit or zoning amendment shall be granted or adopted unless 
the following requirements are met:  
1. The office of community development shall review and calculate the fees for all 
development impact projects. Applicants may request a schedule for the payment of
linkage fees in accordance with regulations established by the community development 
board.  
2. If an applicant elects not to pay the linkage fee as determined by the office of community 
development, then the applicant shall prepare and submit to the office of community 
development an independent fee calculation study for the land development activity for 
which a building or use permit is sought. The independent fee calculation study shall 
show the basis upon which the independent fee calculation was made, and shall follow 
the prescribed methodologies and formats based on regulations promulgated by the 
community development board.  
3. The person or persons making application for a building permit or a density bonus, 
variance, special permit or zoning map amendment to construct, substantially 
rehabilitate, enlarge or extend a structure pursuant to a development impact project plan 
shall also enter into an agreement with the city to pay a park and recreational facilities 
linkage fee. For each development impact project, except for those exemptions found in 
section 94-10.1.4, a park and recreational facilities linkage fee will be paid as reviewed 
and approved by the office of community development.  
4. The building commissioner shall not issue any building or use permit with respect to any 
building, structure, or land within an area covered by a development impact project plan 
until the office of community development provides certification to the building 
commissioner that the applicant has entered into a fee payment agreement as provided 
for herein .  
5. The park and recreational facilities linkage fee shall be paid to, and eventually withdrawn 
from, the park and recreational facilities trust based upon a schedule of fees and rules 
and regulations established by the community development board.  
6. The formula (amount and rate of payment) for the park and recreational facilities linkage 
fee shall be subject to recalculation at leastno more than three years after the effective 
date of this provision, and at leastno more than every three years thereafter. The mayor 
or the office of community developmentcommunity development board, after public 
notice and a public hearing of the Community Development Board, may recalculate and 
amend the formula for the park and recreational facilities linkage fee, based on a 
methodology and analysis established as a result of report(s), documentation and 
information they prepared by a studythe office of community development.  
94-10.1.4 Exemptions. The following are not development impact projects and will not be 
subject to development impact project requirements:  
1. Any structure for which a building or use permit has been lawfully issued prior to the city 
council adopting this division, provided that construction work under such a permit is 
commenced within six months after its issuance, and the work proceeds in good faith 
continuously to completion so far as is reasonably practicable under the circumstances.  
2. Any building, structure, addition or substantial rehabilitation below the thresholds 
described in section 94-10.1.4.
3. Any building, structure, substantial rehabilitation, or addition that is proposed for 
subsidized, or affordable homeowner or rental housing, which falls within criteria 
established by the Commonwealth of Massachusetts or the department of housing and 
urban development, and confirmed by vote of the community development board.  
4. Any building, structure, substantial rehabilitation, or addition that is proposed for: a 
religious or nonprofit educational purpose; a preschool or child care center; a hospital, 
nursing home, associated outpatient clinic or other health care facility licensed by the 
Massachusetts Department of Public Health; a social service center, nonprofit 
community or recreation center, museum, library, art gallery or other public service use.  
5. Any structure, conforming or otherwise, damaged or destroyed by fire or other 
catastrophe where the structure will not be rebuilt beyond its former dimensions.  
6. Any claim of exemption shall be made no later than the time of application for a building 
permit. Any claim not so made shall be deemed waived.  
94-10.1.5 Refund of Linkage Fee Paid. The applicant shall be entitled to a refund of linkage 
fees for a development impact project provided that a written request is submitted to the office of 
community development within six months of the issuance of a building permit, and provided that 
no work has commenced on the project. The request shall be reviewed by the office of community 
development and the linkage fee, minus ten percent to offset the costs of collection and refund, 
may be returned to the applicant. Any funds not expended or encumbered by the end of the 
calendar quarter immediately following six years from the date the linkage fee was paid shall, upon 
application of the applicant or his assign(s), be returned to such landowner provided that the 
applicant or his assign(s) submits an application for a refund to the office of community 
development within 180 days of the expiration of the six-year period.  
94-10.1.6 Credits. A credit may be given for voluntary site-related improvements or 
dedications as approved by the community development board or work performed as required by 
section 94-6.4.  
1. Credit against a linkage fee otherwise due will not be provided until:  
a. The construction is completed and accepted by the city, or the state, whichever is 
applicable.  
b. Security in the form of a performance bond, irrevocable letter of credit, or escrow 
agreement shall be posted with and approved by the office of community 
development.  
c. All design, construction, inspection, testing, bonding and acceptance procedures 
are in strict compliance with the current state and city requirements.  
2. Credit may be provided before completion of specified improvements if adequate 
assurances are given by the applicant that the standards set out in section 94-10.1.6 will 
be met, and if the applicant posts security as provided herein for the costs of such 
construction.
3. Any claim for credit must be made no later than the time of application for a building 
permit. Any claim not so made shall be deemed waived.  
4. Credits shall not be transferable from one project or development to another without the 
approval of the community development board, and may only be transferred to another 
development upon a finding by the community development board that the voluntary 
dedication for which the credit was given equally benefits the city.  
5. Determinations made by the community development board or the office of community 
development pursuant to the linkage fees or credit provision of this section may be 
appealed to the city council by filing a written request with the city council within 30 days 
of the community development board or the office of community development's 
determination. The appeal procedure shall be as provided for in M.G.L.A. c. 40A, § 15.  
94-10.1.7 Penalty. A violation of this section shall be prosecuted in the same manner as 
misdemeanors are prosecuted and upon conviction the violator shall be punishable according to

Sec. 94-10.2. Police and fire facilities. 
94-10.2.1 Purpose. The purpose of this section is to promote the public health, safety, 
convenience and welfare; to prevent overuse and deterioration of existing police and fire facilities; 
to establish a balance between real estate development and the police and fire needs of city 
residents; and to mitigate the impacts of future development on the overuse and deterioration of 
police and fire facilities, and the need for new capital improvements, by provisions designed to:  
1. Afford review and regulation of real estate development projects which directly or 
indirectly lead to conditions of the use of police and fire facilities that contribute to an 
increase in the costs for the upgrade, repair and maintenance of police and fire facilities, 
and the need for new capital improvements.  
2. Provide a fund for police and fire facility capital improvements through a linkage grant to 
the police and fire linkagepark and recreational facilities trust, as a condition of the 
approval of: any nonresidential development of 10,000 square feet of gross floor area or 
more; any residential development of six units or more; any subdivision of property which 
creates six or more units or buildable lots; or any residential or nonresidential project 
requiring a density bonus, variance, special permit, or zoning map amendment that is 
requested for a project of 5,000 square feet or more, except those that are exempt 
pursuant to section 94-10.2.4. Requests for such zoning relief may include bonuses in 
density of use such as increases in gross floor area, height or other changes in 
dimensional requirements.  
3. The imposition of linkage fees is one of the preferred methods of ensuring that 
development bears a proportionate share of the cost of capital facilities necessary to 
accommodate such development. This must be done in order to promote and protect the 
public health, safety and welfare.
4. The methodology and analysis for the determination of the impact of new development, 
the need for new facilities and their costs, and the establishment and calculation of the 
linkage fees shall be established as a result of an investigation and report with supporting 
documentation, which shall be available for inspection by any feepayer or the public.  
Calculations of linkage fees may be based on the methodology established by previous 
studies that outline methods for an escalating linkage fee formula. 
94-10.2.2 Definitions. See section 94-12.0, "Development linkage fees".  
94-10.2.3 Procedures. The mayor or the office of community developmentcommunity 
development board shall be empowered to promulgate regulations and establish fees it deems 
necessary to implement this section. For a development impact project, no building permit or 
density bonus, variance, special permit or zoning amendment shall be granted or adopted unless 
the following are met:  
1. The office of community development shall review and calculate the fees for all 
development impact projects. Applicants may request a schedule for the payment of 
linkage fees in accordance with regulations established by the community development 
board.  
2. If an applicant elects not to pay the linkage fee as determined by office of community 
development, then the applicant shall prepare and submit to the office of community 
development an independent fee calculation study for the land development activity for 
which a building or use permit is sought. The independent fee calculation study shall 
show the basis upon which the independent fee calculation was made, and shall follow 
the prescribed methodologies and formats based on regulations promulgated by the 
community development board.  
3. The person or persons making application for a building permit or a density bonus, 
variance, special permit, or zoning map amendment to construct, substantially 
rehabilitate, enlarge or extend a structure pursuant to a development impact project plan

fee. For each development impact project, except for those exemptions found in section 
94-10.2.4, a police and fire facilities linkage fee will be paid as reviewed and approved by 
the office of community development.

building, structure, or land within an area covered by a development impact project plan 
until the office of community development provides certification to the building 
commissioner that the applicant has entered into a fee payment agreement.

the police and fire facilities trust based upon a schedule of fees and rules and 
regulations established by the community development board.

of this provision, and at leastno more than every three years thereafter. The mayor or the 
office of community developmentcommunity development board, after public notice
and a public hearing of the Community Development Board, may recalculate and amend 
the formula for the police and fire facilities linkage fee, based on a methodology and

commenced within six months after its issuance, and the work proceeds in good faith 
continuously to completion so far as is reasonably practicable under the circumstances.

urban development, and confirmed by vote of the city community development board.

community or recreation center, museum, library, art gallery or other public service use.

development.

to another development upon a finding by the community development board that the

5. Determinations made by the community development board or the office of

may be appealed to the city council by filing a written request with the city council within 
30 days of the community development board or the office of community development's 
determination. The appeal procedure shall be as provided for in M.G.L.A. c. 40A, § 15.  
94-10.5.7 Penalty. A violation of this section shall be prosecuted in the same manner as 
misdemeanors are prosecuted and upon conviction the violator shall be punishable according to

RE: Draft Updated Combined Sewer Overflow Long-Term Control Plan Public Comment 
 
Dear MWRA, Cambridge, and Somerville Combined Sewer Overflow Project Team, 
On behalf of the City of Medford City Council, we respectfully request that you reject the 
Recommended Plan presented in the Draft Updated Combined Sewer Overflow (CSO) Long-
Term Control Plan (LTCP) that would allow sewage to be discharged permanently into the 
Mystic River, Charles River, and Alewife Brook, a proposal we find unacceptable. We strongly 
oppose any plan that permits continued pollution of our local waterways and urge you to issue a 
Final Updated CSO Control Plan that recommends an alternative resulting in complete or 
virtual CSO elimination. Massachusetts can and should do better. 
 
While the Boston Harbor and our waterways have seen a remarkable recovery thanks to 
decades of public investment, this progress is now at risk. The Draft LTCP would allow raw 
sewage dumping into our rivers indefinitely, when instead we should be investing in safe, clean, 
and healthy waterways that residents expect and deserve. Our rivers should not be treated as 
open sewers, especially when modern infrastructure solutions are feasible and available. 
The Draft Recommended Plan is inadequate in the following ways:
31 
 
• It fails to meet federal Clean Water Act requirements; 
• It fails to end CSOs despite analysis demonstrating it is both technically feasible and 
affordable; 
• It is backward-looking and proposes investments in infrastructure that will be 
overwhelmed by current and future climate conditions; 
• It fails to acknowledge the public health and economic benefits that would be realized 
from ending CSOs; and 
• It fails to advance state priorities as detailed in the Healey-Driscoll Administration’s 
Biodiversity Initiative, Environmental Justice Strategy, and ResilientMass Plan.  
 
Medford and neighboring communities along the Mystic River have worked for decades and 
continue to work to restore these waterways. Our city is required to make considerable 
investments to address stormwater runoff into the river, and we are working hard on a daily 
basis to meet those obligations. Allowing some entities to permanently discharge sewage in the 
Mystic undermines these efforts and is not equitable. Discharges of raw sewage degrade 
habitat, impair water quality, limit safe recreation, and threaten public health—impacts that fall 
disproportionately on Environmental Justice communities already burdened by pollution. 
At a time when climate change is increasing storm intensity and placing greater stress on our 
infrastructure, we must pursue solutions that meet future conditions rather than waste money on 
outdated approaches. The Draft Control Plan demonstrates that you have the capacity and 
expertise to permanently end raw sewage discharges into our rivers; the City of Medford is 
asking you to make that commitment. 
 
We respectfully request that you recommend and implement a 2050, 25-year storm level of 
control or full sewer separation for the Mystic River, the Charles River, and the Alewife 
Brook under the Final Updated LTCP. A 25-year level of control is analogous to what was done 
for Boston Harbor beaches, while discharges have been fully eliminated on the Neponset River. 
We have a unique opportunity to end CSOs in our beloved waterways so we can finally achieve 
the vision of the federal Clean Water Act for “fishable” and “swimmable” rivers. We urge you to 
ensure that the MWRA continues its legacy of leadership in CSO reduction by supporting a plan 
that permanently ends sewage dumping into the Mystic River, Charles River, and Alewife Brook.
